title: Trust stores and what servers send
summary: Where roots live on Windows and elsewhere, and why a server must send its intermediates.

steps.title: The trust store
body: The end of every chain is a **trust anchor**: a root certificate your machine has decided to trust. Those live in a **trust store**.
On Windows the certificate store has two locations and several folders:
| Store path | Shown as | Holds |
| `Cert:\LocalMachine\Root` | Trusted Root Certification Authorities | roots trusted by the whole machine |
| `Cert:\LocalMachine\CA` | Intermediate Certification Authorities | intermediates (a cache, not anchors) |
| `Cert:\LocalMachine\My` | Personal | certificates **with private keys** that this machine uses (IIS, services) |
| `Cert:\CurrentUser\...` | the same folders, per user | trust and identities for one user only |
```text
PS> Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter
PS> Get-ChildItem Cert:\CurrentUser\My
PS> certutil -store Root
Other worlds keep their own lists: Linux in `/etc/ssl/certs` (update with `update-ca-certificates`), Java in a `cacerts`
keystore, Firefox in its own store, and a Docker image in whatever its base image shipped.

steps.prompt: Match each Windows store to what you'd find there.
pairs: the IIS site's certificate and its private key
a root trusted only for your user account

prompt: Your internal API uses a certificate from the company's own root CA. Calls work from your Windows laptop,
but the same code in a **Linux Docker container** fails with `RemoteCertificateChainErrors`. Most likely cause?
options: The container's trust store doesn't contain the company root; IT pushed it to Windows machines only
The certificate is expired in the container's time zone
steps.explain: Domain-joined Windows machines get corporate roots by Group Policy. A container starts from its base image's store. Copy the root into `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/` and run `update-ca-certificates` in the Dockerfile.

steps.title: The server must send the intermediates
body: The client has the **roots**. It usually does *not* have every intermediate. So in the TLS handshake the server sends:
```text
leaf  ->  intermediate(s)       (the root is optional; the client has it or it's no use)
Forgetting the intermediate is one of the most common TLS mistakes, and a sneaky one, because some clients paper over it:
- **Windows and browsers** often have the intermediate **cached** from another site, or download it via the leaf's
*Authority Information Access* URL. It works on your machine.
- **Mobile apps, Java, curl, Linux and .NET on Linux** often don't. It fails there.
That is why CAs hand you a `fullchain.pem` (leaf + intermediates). Configure the server with that file, not with `cert.pem` alone.

prompt: Users on Android report `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID` on your new site. On your Windows laptop Chrome shows a padlock.
The certificate is from a well-known public CA and not expired. What is most likely wrong?
options: The server sends only the leaf, not the intermediate; your laptop has the intermediate cached, the phone does not
Android doesn't trust that CA's root
The certificate's SAN is missing the www name
steps.explain: "Works here, fails there" with a public CA is the classic missing-intermediate signature. Fix the server to send the full chain. Online checkers like SSL Labs flag it as *Chain issues: Incomplete*.

steps.prompt: In a TLS handshake for `shop.example`, what should the server send?
items: the root certificate (it's useless: clients must already have it)
steps.explain: Sending the root is harmless but pointless: a client only trusts a root it already has. Private keys never leave the server.

steps.prompt: `X509Chain` builds chains in .NET. Here the trust store is replaced by our own root, and `ExtraStore` plays the role of "certificates the server sent". What does it print?
code: var root = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true);
var inter = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", root, true);
Console.WriteLine(chain.Build(leaf));          // server sent only the leaf
chain.ChainPolicy.ExtraStore.Add(inter);        // server sent the intermediate too
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
steps.explain: Without the intermediate there is no path from the leaf to the root. With it, the chain is leaf, intermediate, root: three elements.

steps.title: Does the chain validate?
prompt: Write `bool Validates(X509Certificate2 leaf, List<X509Certificate2> sent, X509Certificate2 root)` that returns whether
`leaf` chains up to `root`, using **only** `root` as the trust anchor and the `sent` certificates as extra candidates.
Set up an `X509Chain` like the previous step:
- `VerificationTime = new DateTime(2031, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)` (the test certificates are valid 2030 to 2035)
starter: bool Validates(X509Certificate2 leaf, List<X509Certificate2> sent, X509Certificate2 root)
solution: bool Validates(X509Certificate2 leaf, List<X509Certificate2> sent, X509Certificate2 root)
template: var dojoRoot = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true);
var dojoInter = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", dojoRoot, true);
var dojoEvil = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true);
Dojo.Eq("leaf + intermediate sent: valid", true, Validates(dojoLeaf, new List<X509Certificate2> { dojoInter }, dojoRoot));
Dojo.Eq("only the leaf sent: not valid", false, Validates(dojoLeaf, new List<X509Certificate2>(), dojoRoot));
Dojo.Eq("trusting a different root with the same name: not valid", false, Validates(dojoLeaf, new List<X509Certificate2> { dojoInter }, dojoEvil));
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
